szoveg_eredeti:
Artificial Intelligence Outperformed Nephrologists in Recalling Rare Kidney Disease Trial Data

An evaluation comparing artificial intelligence models with practicing nephrologists found that machine learning tools achieved significantly higher accuracy when recalling specific clinical trial outcomes in rare kidney diseases. In an online survey conducted among medical specialists, four major artificial intelligence systems demonstrated an overall median accuracy of 95 percent, notably outperforming human clinicians who attained a median accuracy of 50 percent. The study evaluated how effectively digital models and human physicians retrieve detailed endpoints from landmark nephrology studies, addressing an operational environment where clinical literature expands continuously and poses substantial cognitive retention challenges for practitioners managing complex renal disorders.

The investigation was conducted during the Loma Linda University Rare Kidney Disease conference held in Palm Springs, California, in December 2024. Researchers distributed an online survey link to conference participants to evaluate response accuracy across selected trial outcomes. Of the 449 clinicians attending the conference, 46 nephrologists completed the survey, representing a response rate of 10.2 percent. The participating physicians brought established clinical backgrounds, reporting a median duration of practice since completing nephrology specialty training of 5 years, with an interquartile range spanning from 2 to 10 years. Preliminary findings from the project were subsequently shared at the European Renal Association 2025 Congress in Vienna, Austria.

To construct the knowledge assessment, researchers designed a 10-question questionnaire derived from 11 recent and landmark clinical trials focused on specialized kidney conditions. The selected investigations addressed major renal pathologies, specifically IgA nephropathy, lupus nephritis, C3 glomerulopathy, and polycystic kidney disease. Across the questionnaire, nine questions evaluated data from individual clinical trials, while one question evaluated data combined across two separate investigations. This structure tested detailed recall of trial parameters and therapeutic outcomes that nephrologists encounter when reviewing peer-reviewed evidence for rare disease management.

The landmark investigations selected for the survey represented high-impact nephrology research that has shaped current clinical discussions. Research on polycystic kidney disease was incorporated through questions referencing the TEMPO 3:4 and REPRISE studies, providing a broad testing base across complex nephrology literature.

To evaluate machine performance against human clinicians, the identical 10-question survey was submitted to four prominent artificial intelligence models representing different capability tiers and accessibility structures. The models assessed included Google’s Gemini 1.5 Flash and OpenAI’s ChatGPT-4, both operating under their free-access tiers, as well as Gemini 1.5 Pro and ChatGPT-4 Turbo, representing advanced paid-tier architectures. All four models were tested through their standard web interfaces at the time the evaluation was executed. Researchers recorded the generated outputs from each model and compared the correctness of their responses against the answers submitted by the 46 participating nephrologists.

Comparative analysis revealed that artificial intelligence systems achieved significantly superior overall accuracy relative to the surveyed nephrologists. Across the full questionnaire, artificial intelligence models attained a median accuracy of 95 percent, with an interquartile range of 85 to 100 percent, whereas the human nephrologists achieved a median accuracy of 50 percent, with an interquartile range between 30 and 80 percent, yielding a statistically significant difference with a P value of 0.008. When individual questions were analyzed, no statistically significant performance differences were observed for the majority of the prompts; however, artificial intelligence outperformed human participants in answering a subset of specific questions with greater factual accuracy.

The authors emphasized that the observed findings must be interpreted with caution due to several methodological constraints. The survey examined a relatively small cohort of 46 clinicians from a single meeting, representing a 10.2 percent response rate, and utilized a concise 10-question instrument. Consequently, the researchers noted that the findings should be regarded as preliminary and hypothesis-generating. Furthermore, because testing took place in December 2024, the study reflects a period when concerns regarding model hallucinations and factual reliability were widespread among healthcare professionals, although the evaluated models demonstrated consistent recall without major errors when queried about well-established, high-impact clinical trials.

In discussing the broader relevance of their observations, the researchers noted that retaining detailed data from growing numbers of clinical trials presents an escalating challenge for practicing clinicians. As the volume of evidence in rare kidney disease continues to expand, relying exclusively on human memory to recall precise trial metrics and primary endpoints may become increasingly impractical. The study authors concluded that their findings support a complementary workflow model where artificial intelligence systems serve as an efficient adjunct for retrieving structured trial data on demand, while specialized clinical expertise remains indispensable for interpreting evidence and guiding clinical decision-making.

Subject of Research: Evaluation of artificial intelligence versus nephrologists in recalling rare kidney disease clinical trial data

Article Title: Can artificial intelligence outperform clinicians in recalling rare kidney diseases clinical trial data?

Article References: Ebrahimi, N., Vakhshoori, M., Abdipour, A., Chowdhury, R., Heidari-Bateni, G., Garimella, P. S., Shah, S., & Norouzi, S. (2026). Can artificial intelligence outperform clinicians in recalling rare kidney diseases clinical trial data?. Rare Kidney Diseases, 1(1), Article 3. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44531-026-00003-5
